2 Kings 1.summary: After the death of Ahab, Moab rebels against Israel (2 Kings 1:1). Ahaziah falls down through a lattice in his upper room in Samaria and sends messengers to ask Baalzebub the god of Ekron whether he will recover (2 Kings 1:2). Elijah meets the messengers and asks, "Is it not because there is not a God in Israel," and tells them the king shall surely die (2 Kings 1:3–8). Ahaziah sends a captain with fifty men, then a second, and fire comes down from heaven and burns up both companies (2 Kings 1:9–12). The third captain falls on his knees and begs for his life, and the angel of the LORD tells Elijah to go with him and not be afraid (2 Kings 1:13–15). Elijah tells Ahaziah to his face that he shall die, and he dies, and Jehoram reigns in his place because he has no son (2 Kings 1:16–18).
2 Kings 1.whereWeAre: 1 Kings ended with Ahaziah reigning in Israel and doing evil like his father Ahab. 2 Kings opens with that same king, hurt in a fall and asking a foreign god whether he will live, while Elijah answers him in the name of the LORD. Chapter 2 tells how Elijah is taken up and Elisha takes his place.

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who falls from his upper room and asks Baalzebub if he will recover.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Meets the messengers, calls down fire on two companies, and tells the king he will die.

keyFigures.name: The first two captains
keyFigures.role: Each comes with fifty men to say the king wants Elijah to come down.

keyFigures.name: The third captain
keyFigures.role: Falls on his knees and begs for his life.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Sends Elijah to the messengers and tells him to go with the third captain.

keyThemes.explanation: Elijah asks if there is no God in Israel, that the king sends to Baalzebub of Ekron.

keyThemes.theme: The word of the LORD stands
keyThemes.explanation: Ahaziah dies "according to the word of the LORD which Elijah had spoken."

keyThemes.theme: Pride and a plea for mercy
keyThemes.explanation: Two captains order a prophet to come down and are burned up, while the third begs for his life and is spared.

2 Kings 2.summary: The LORD is about to take Elijah up into heaven by a whirlwind, and Elijah and Elisha go from Gilgal to Bethel, to Jericho, and to the Jordan, and each time Elisha says, "I will not leave thee" (2 Kings 2:1–6). Elijah strikes the waters with his mantle and they cross on dry ground (2 Kings 2:7–8). Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit, and a chariot of fire and horses of fire part them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven (2 Kings 2:9–12). Elisha takes up the mantle that fell from Elijah, strikes the waters, and says, "Where is the LORD God of Elijah?" and they part, and the sons of the prophets say, "The spirit of Elijah doth rest on Elisha" (2 Kings 2:13–18). At the request of the men of Jericho he throws salt into the spring and heals the waters (2 Kings 2:19–22). Little children come out of Bethel and mock him, saying, "Go up, thou bald head," and he curses them in the name of the LORD, and two she bears tear forty-two of them (2 Kings 2:23–25).
2 Kings 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Ahaziah dead and Jehoram on the throne. This chapter tells how Elijah is taken up into heaven in a whirlwind, and how Elisha takes his mantle, divides the Jordan, and begins his own work. Chapter 3 shows Elisha helping three kings in the war with Moab.

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Crosses the Jordan, is parted from Elisha by a chariot of fire, and goes up in a whirlwind.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Refuses to leave Elijah, takes up the mantle, and heals the water of Jericho.

keyFigures.name: The sons of the prophets
keyFigures.role: Tell Elisha his master will be taken, and later say the spirit of Elijah rests on him.

keyFigures.name: The men of Jericho
keyFigures.role: Ask Elisha to heal the bad water.

keyFigures.name: The children at Bethel
keyFigures.role: Mock Elisha on the way.

keyThemes.explanation: Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit and takes up his mantle.
Three times Elisha says, "I will not leave thee."

keyThemes.theme: The LORD answers through his prophet
keyThemes.explanation: The waters part and the spring is healed in the name of the LORD, but those who mock the prophet are cursed.

2 Kings 3.summary: Jehoram the son of Ahab reigns in Israel and puts away the image of Baal that his father had made, but holds to the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 3:1–3). Mesha king of Moab, who paid a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams, rebels, so Jehoram asks Jehoshaphat to go with him, and the king of Edom joins them (2 Kings 3:4–9). After a seven days' journey there is no water for the army or the cattle, and Jehoshaphat asks, "Is there not here a prophet of the LORD?" (2 Kings 3:9–12). Elisha says that were it not for Jehoshaphat he would not look toward Jehoram, and when the minstrel plays, the hand of the LORD comes on him, and he says, "Make this valley full of ditches" (2 Kings 3:13–20). In the morning water comes by way of Edom, and the Moabites see it red as blood and say, "This is blood," and think the kings are slain, and Israel strikes them (2 Kings 3:20–25). The king of Moab takes his eldest son and offers him as a burnt offering on the wall, and there is great anger against Israel, and they go home (2 Kings 3:26–27).
2 Kings 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with Elisha going on after Elijah. This chapter shows the first test of that work, when Israel, Judah, and Edom march against Moab, run out of water, and Elisha tells them to dig ditches. Chapter 4 turns to Elisha's help for ordinary people.

keyFigures.name: Jehoram of Israel
keyFigures.role: Gathers the three kings against Moab but still follows Jeroboam's sins.

keyFigures.name: Jehoshaphat
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who asks for a prophet of the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The king of Edom
keyFigures.role: Joins the march and goes with them to Elisha.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Tells them to make the valley full of ditches, and promises water and victory.

keyFigures.name: Mesha king of Moab
keyFigures.role: Rebels, loses the battle, and offers his eldest son on the wall.

keyThemes.theme: Asking for the word of the LORD
keyThemes.explanation: Only when the water fails do the kings look for a prophet, and Elisha helps for Jehoshaphat's sake.
The valley is filled with water without wind or rain, and it is "a light thing in the sight of the LORD."
Mesha's sacrifice of his son brings great anger against Israel, and the three kings go home.

2 Kings 4.summary: The widow of one of the sons of the prophets cries to Elisha that the creditor has come to take her two sons as servants, and all she has is a pot of oil (2 Kings 4:1–2). Elisha tells her to borrow empty vessels, not a few, and the oil keeps flowing until every vessel is full, and she sells it and pays her debt (2 Kings 4:3–7). A great woman of Shunem makes a little room on the wall for Elisha, and he promises her a son, who is born the next year (2 Kings 4:8–17). The child goes out to his father in the field, cries, "My head, my head," and dies on his mother's knees (2 Kings 4:18–20). She goes to Elisha at mount Carmel, and Elisha lies on the child, who sneezes seven times and opens his eyes (2 Kings 4:21–37). At Gilgal in a famine, Elisha heals the pot of stew with meal when the sons of the prophets cry, "there is death in the pot" (2 Kings 4:38–41). He feeds a hundred men with twenty loaves of barley, and they eat and have some left, according to the word of the LORD (2 Kings 4:42–44).
2 Kings 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with the war against Moab. This chapter shows Elisha helping people at home: a widow in debt, a woman of Shunem whose son dies, a pot of bad stew, and a hundred hungry men. Chapter 5 tells of the healing of Naaman.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Fills the widow's vessels with oil, raises the Shunammite's son, heals the pot, and feeds a hundred men.

keyFigures.name: The prophet's widow
keyFigures.role: Pours out her little oil into borrowed vessels.

keyFigures.name: The Shunammite woman
keyFigures.role: Builds a room for Elisha and goes to him when her son dies.

keyFigures.name: Gehazi
keyFigures.role: Elisha's servant, who lays the staff on the child's face with no result.

keyFigures.name: The Shunammite's son
keyFigures.role: Dies in the field and is brought back to life.

keyThemes.explanation: A small pot of oil pays the widow's creditor and keeps her sons.
The woman who gave Elisha a room receives a son, loses him, and gets him back.
Meal heals the stew, and twenty loaves feed a hundred men with food left over.

2 Kings 5.summary: Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Syria, is a great man and a mighty man in valour, "but he was a leper" (2 Kings 5:1). A little maid taken captive out of Israel says to her mistress, "Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria," and the king of Syria sends him with a letter, and the king of Israel tears his clothes (2 Kings 5:2–7). Elisha says, "let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel" (2 Kings 5:8–10). Naaman is angry that Elisha will not come out, but his servants say that if the prophet had asked him to do some great thing he would have done it, and he dips seven times in the Jordan and is clean (2 Kings 5:11–14). He says, "now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel," and Elisha refuses a gift (2 Kings 5:15–19). Gehazi runs after Naaman, takes a talent of silver and two changes of clothes, and lies to Elisha, and the leprosy of Naaman clings to him, and he goes out a leper as white as snow (2 Kings 5:20–27).
2 Kings 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with Elisha feeding a hundred men. This chapter tells how a foreign army captain is healed of leprosy by washing in the Jordan, and how Elisha's own servant Gehazi is struck with it for his greed. Chapter 6 returns to the war between Syria and Israel.

keyFigures.name: Naaman
keyFigures.role: Syrian captain, who is angry at first, then washes seven times and is healed.

keyFigures.name: The little maid
keyFigures.role: A captive Israelite girl who tells Naaman's wife about the prophet.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Sends word to wash in the Jordan and refuses a reward.

keyFigures.name: Naaman's servants
keyFigures.role: Persuade him to do the simple thing.

keyFigures.name: Gehazi
keyFigures.role: Takes silver and clothes by a lie and is struck with leprosy.

keyThemes.explanation: A captive girl and Naaman's own servants lead him to healing.
Naaman wants a grand show, but is healed when he washes seven times as told.

keyThemes.theme: A free gift and a greedy servant
keyThemes.explanation: Elisha takes nothing, but Gehazi takes a reward and lies about it.

2 Kings 6.summary: The sons of the prophets cut beams at the Jordan, and an axe head falls into the water, and Elisha throws in a stick and makes the iron swim (2 Kings 6:1–7). Elisha tells the king of Israel where Syria is hiding to ambush him, and the king of Syria sends horses and chariots and a great army to Dothan by night (2 Kings 6:8–14). Elisha's servant says, "Alas, my master! how shall we do?" and Elisha says, "Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them," and the young man sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). The LORD strikes the Syrians with blindness, Elisha leads them to Samaria, and the king of Israel sets bread and water before them and sends them home (2 Kings 6:18–23). Afterward Benhadad gathers all his army and besieges Samaria, and there is a great famine, so that a donkey's head is sold for eighty pieces of silver (2 Kings 6:24–25). A woman cries to the king about a bargain to eat her son, and the king tears his clothes, with sackcloth underneath, and swears to take off Elisha's head (2 Kings 6:26–33).
2 Kings 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 ended with Gehazi's leprosy. This chapter shows Elisha helping the sons of the prophets and Israel's king, surrounded at Dothan by a Syrian army and a heavenly one, and then Samaria under siege and famine, with the king blaming Elisha. Chapter 7 gives the answer.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Floats the axe head, opens his servant's eyes, and leads the Syrians to Samaria.

keyFigures.name: Elisha's servant
keyFigures.role: Sees the army and is afraid, then sees the chariots of fire.

keyFigures.name: The king of Israel
keyFigures.role: Feeds the Syrians and sends them home, then blames Elisha in the famine.

keyFigures.name: The king of Syria
keyFigures.role: Sends an army to Dothan, then Benhadad besieges Samaria.

keyFigures.name: The woman in Samaria
keyFigures.role: Cries to the king about the son she and her neighbour agreed to eat.

keyThemes.theme: The LORD cares about small losses
keyThemes.explanation: A borrowed axe head is brought back to the top of the water.

keyThemes.theme: More with us than against us
keyThemes.explanation: The mountain is full of horses and chariots of fire "round about Elisha."
The Syrians are fed and sent home instead of killed, and the raiders come no more.

2 Kings 7.summary: Elisha says, "Hear ye the word of the LORD," and promises that tomorrow about this time a measure of fine flour will sell for a shekel in the gate of Samaria, and a lord on whose hand the king leans says even if the LORD made windows in heaven, this could not be (2 Kings 7:1–2). Elisha answers, "thou shalt see it with thine eyes, but shalt not eat thereof" (2 Kings 7:2). Four leprous men at the entrance of the gate decide to go to the army of the Syrians, and when they come they find no man there (2 Kings 7:3–5). The LORD had made the Syrians hear a noise of chariots and horses, and they fled for their lives and left the camp as it was (2 Kings 7:6–8). The lepers say, "We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace," and they tell the king's household (2 Kings 7:9–11). The king sends two chariot horsemen who find the way full of clothes and vessels the Syrians threw away, and the people plunder the tents (2 Kings 7:12–16). The lord is set to keep the gate, and the people trample him and he dies, as the man of God had said (2 Kings 7:17–20).
2 Kings 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 ended with Samaria starving and the king angry with Elisha. This chapter gives Elisha's answer: food will be cheap by tomorrow, four lepers find the Syrian camp empty, and an officer who doubted sees the plenty but dies at the gate. Chapter 8 returns to the Shunammite woman and to Hazael.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Promises plenty by tomorrow and tells the doubting lord he will not eat of it.

keyFigures.name: The four leprous men
keyFigures.role: Go to the Syrian camp, find it empty, and take the news to the city.

keyFigures.name: The king of Israel
keyFigures.role: Fears a trap, but sends horsemen to see.

keyFigures.name: The lord on whose hand the king leaned
keyFigures.role: Doubts that it can happen and is trampled to death at the gate.

keyThemes.explanation: The flour and barley sell for a shekel just as the man of God had said.
The lepers say, "We do not well," and go back to tell the city.
The lord who doubted the promise sees the food and does not eat of it.

2 Kings 8.summary: Elisha tells the woman whose son he restored to go away, because the LORD has called for a famine, and she stays in the land of the Philistines seven years (2 Kings 8:1–2). When she returns and cries to the king for her house and land, Gehazi is telling the king how Elisha restored a dead body to life, and the king restores all that was hers (2 Kings 8:3–6). Elisha comes to Damascus, where Benhadad is sick, and Hazael goes to meet him with forty camels carrying every good thing of Damascus (2 Kings 8:7–9). Elisha tells him the king shall surely die, and weeps, saying he knows the evil Hazael will do to the children of Israel, and Hazael says, "But what, is thy servant a dog" (2 Kings 8:10–13). The next day Hazael takes a thick cloth, dips it in water, spreads it on the king's face, and reigns in his place (2 Kings 8:14–15). Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat reigns eight years in Judah and walks in the way of the house of Ahab, because Ahab's daughter is his wife, and Edom revolts (2 Kings 8:16–22). His son Ahaziah reigns one year and goes with Joram to war against Hazael, and visits Joram at Jezreel when he is wounded (2 Kings 8:23–29).
2 Kings 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 ended with the doubting lord trampled at the gate. This chapter shows the Shunammite woman getting her land back, Elisha foretelling that Hazael will be king of Syria, and the kings of Judah, Jehoram and Ahaziah, joined to the house of Ahab. Chapter 9 tells how Jehu is anointed.

keyFigures.name: The Shunammite woman
keyFigures.role: Leaves for seven years in famine and returns to ask for her house and land.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Tells Hazael he will be king and weeps at the evil he will do.

keyFigures.name: Gehazi
keyFigures.role: Is telling the king of Elisha's wonders when the woman comes in.

keyFigures.name: Hazael
keyFigures.role: Brings a present to Elisha, then kills Benhadad and reigns.

keyFigures.name: Jehoram of Judah
keyFigures.role: Marries Ahab's daughter and walks in the ways of Israel's kings.

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah of Judah
keyFigures.role: Follows the house of Ahab and visits Joram at Jezreel.

keyThemes.explanation: The king is asking about Elisha's wonders at the moment the woman arrives.
Elisha weeps because he knows what Hazael will do to Israel.
Jehoram and Ahaziah walk in the way of the house of Ahab through marriage.

2 Kings 9.summary: Elisha calls one of the sons of the prophets and sends him with a box of oil to Ramothgilead to anoint Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi king over Israel (2 Kings 9:1–6). He says, "Thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets," and the dogs shall eat Jezebel in the portion of Jezreel (2 Kings 9:7–10). The captains ask, "wherefore came this mad fellow to thee?" and then they blow the trumpet and say, "Jehu is king" (2 Kings 9:11–13). Jehu rides in a chariot to Jezreel, driving furiously, and meets Joram, who asks, "Is it peace, Jehu?" and Jehu says, "What peace, so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?" (2 Kings 9:14–22). Jehu draws a bow with all his strength and strikes Joram, whose body is thrown into the field of Naboth, and Ahaziah of Judah is also struck and dies at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:23–29). Jezebel paints her face, and Jehu says, "Throw her down," and the dogs eat her, so that they find no more of her than the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands (2 Kings 9:30–37).
2 Kings 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with Ahaziah of Judah visiting the wounded Joram at Jezreel. This chapter tells how Jehu is anointed in secret, rides to Jezreel, and kills Joram, Ahaziah, and Jezebel, as the LORD had said through Elijah. Chapter 10 tells how he finishes the house of Ahab.

keyFigures.name: Jehu
keyFigures.role: Anointed king, then drives furiously to Jezreel and kills Joram.

keyFigures.name: The young prophet
keyFigures.role: Anoints Jehu with the box of oil and then flees.

keyFigures.name: Joram
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, wounded and killed in the field of Naboth.

keyFigures.name: Ahaziah of Judah
keyFigures.role: Flees to Megiddo and dies there.

keyFigures.name: Jezebel
keyFigures.role: Paints her face, looks out of the window, and is thrown down.

keyThemes.theme: The word of Elijah comes true
keyThemes.explanation: Joram is thrown into the field of Naboth and the dogs eat Jezebel, as the LORD had said.
The captains blow the trumpet and say, "Jehu is king."
Jehu is told to avenge the blood of the prophets and servants of the LORD.

2 Kings 10.summary: Ahab has seventy sons in Samaria, and Jehu writes to the rulers of the city to pick the best of them and fight for their master's house, but they are very afraid and say, "We will not make any king" (2 Kings 10:1–5). Jehu writes again, and they take the king's sons and kill seventy persons and put their heads in baskets, and he lays them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate (2 Kings 10:6–8). He kills all who remain of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, and meets Jehonadab the son of Rechab and asks, "Is thine heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?" and takes him up into his chariot (2 Kings 10:9–17). Jehu cleverly says Ahab served Baal a little but Jehu shall serve him much, and gathers all the worshippers into the house of Baal and has them killed (2 Kings 10:18–25). They break down the image and the house of Baal and make it a latrine, and so Jehu destroys Baal out of Israel (2 Kings 10:26–28). Yet he does not turn from the golden calves at Bethel and Dan, and takes no heed to walk in the law of the LORD with all his heart (2 Kings 10:29–31). In those days the LORD begins to cut Israel short, and Hazael strikes them in all their borders, and Jehu reigns twenty-eight years (2 Kings 10:32–36).
2 Kings 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 ended with Jezebel's death at Jezreel. This chapter shows Jehu killing Ahab's seventy sons and the worshippers of Baal, but keeping the golden calves, so that the LORD begins to cut Israel short through Hazael. Chapter 11 turns to Judah, where Athaliah seizes the throne.

keyFigures.name: Jehu
keyFigures.role: Has Ahab's sons and Baal's worshippers killed but keeps Jeroboam's calves.

keyFigures.name: The rulers of Samaria
keyFigures.role: Are afraid, and kill Ahab's seventy sons at Jehu's word.

keyFigures.name: Jehonadab the son of Rechab
keyFigures.role: Joins Jehu in his chariot and watches his zeal for the LORD.

keyFigures.name: The worshippers of Baal
keyFigures.role: Gathered into the house of Baal and killed.

keyFigures.name: Hazael
keyFigures.role: King of Syria, who strikes the borders of Israel.

keyThemes.explanation: Jehu destroys Baal out of Israel, but "took no heed to walk in the law of the LORD God of Israel with all his heart."
The LORD says Jehu's sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.
The LORD begins to cut Israel short, and Hazael strikes them in all their borders.

2 Kings 11.summary: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah sees that her son is dead, she rises and destroys all the royal seed (2 Kings 11:1). Jehosheba, the daughter of king Joram and sister of Ahaziah, takes Joash the son of Ahaziah and hides him with his nurse in the house of the LORD six years (2 Kings 11:2–3). In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest brings the captains and the guard into the house of the LORD, makes a covenant with them, and shows them the king's son (2 Kings 11:4–8). He brings out the king's son, puts the crown on him, gives him the testimony, and they anoint him and clap their hands and say, "God save the king" (2 Kings 11:9–12). Athaliah hears the noise, comes to the people in the temple, tears her clothes, and cries, "Treason, Treason," and they lay hands on her at the horses' entry and kill her (2 Kings 11:13–16). Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people that they should be the LORD's people, and the people break down the house of Baal and kill Mattan the priest (2 Kings 11:17–18). Joash, seven years old, sits on the throne, and the city is quiet (2 Kings 11:19–21).
2 Kings 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 ended with Jehu's reign in Israel. This chapter turns to Judah, where Athaliah kills the royal seed, Joash is hidden in the temple for six years, and Jehoiada the priest crowns him at seven and ends her rule. Chapter 12 tells how Joash repairs the temple.

keyFigures.name: Athaliah
keyFigures.role: Destroys the royal seed and reigns six years, until she is killed.

keyFigures.name: Jehosheba
keyFigures.role: Steals Joash away and hides him in the house of the LORD.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.role: Hidden as a baby and crowned at seven.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiada the priest
keyFigures.role: Plans the crowning, makes the covenant, and has the temple of Baal broken down.

keyFigures.name: The captains and the guard
keyFigures.role: Stand round the king with weapons and keep Athaliah out.

keyThemes.explanation: A baby is hidden for six years while Athaliah destroys the rest of David's house.
Jehoiada makes a covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people.
Athaliah cries, "Treason, Treason," and is killed at the horses' entry.

2 Kings 12.summary: Joash begins to reign in the seventh year of Jehu and does right in the sight of the LORD all his days while Jehoiada the priest instructs him, but the high places are not taken away (2 Kings 12:1–3). He tells the priests to take the money for the house of the LORD and repair the breaches, but in the twenty-third year the priests have still not repaired the breaches (2 Kings 12:4–6). Jehoiada takes a chest, bores a hole in the lid, and sets it beside the altar, and the money is counted and given to the workmen, who deal faithfully (2 Kings 12:7–16). Hazael king of Syria fights against Gath, takes it, and sets his face to go up to Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:17). Joash takes all the holy things and the gold in the treasures of the house of the LORD and sends it to Hazael, who goes away from Jerusalem (2 Kings 12:18). His servants plot against Joash and kill him in the house of Millo, and Amaziah his son reigns in his place (2 Kings 12:19–21).
2 Kings 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 ended with Joash crowned and the city quiet. This chapter tells how he repairs the temple with the help of Jehoiada, then pays Hazael with temple treasure, and is killed by his own servants. Chapter 13 returns to Israel and to Elisha's last days.

keyFigures.name: Joash
keyFigures.role: Repairs the temple while Jehoiada lives, then pays off Hazael and is killed.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiada the priest
keyFigures.role: Instructs the king and sets the chest by the altar.

keyFigures.name: The priests
keyFigures.role: Fail to repair the house for twenty-three years.

keyFigures.name: The workmen
keyFigures.role: Carpenters, builders, and masons who deal faithfully.

keyFigures.name: Hazael
keyFigures.role: King of Syria, who takes Gath and goes up against Jerusalem.

keyThemes.explanation: Joash does right "all his days wherein Jehoiada the priest instructed him."
The chest by the altar and the faithful workmen get the repairs done.
Joash sends the holy things and the temple gold to Hazael.

2 Kings 13.summary: Jehoahaz son of Jehu reigns seventeen years in Samaria and follows the sins of Jeroboam, so the LORD gives Israel into the hand of Hazael king of Syria (2 Kings 13:1–3). Jehoahaz begs the LORD, and the LORD gives Israel a saviour, so that they live in their tents as before, but they do not turn from the sins of Jeroboam (2 Kings 13:4–9). Joash his son reigns sixteen years and does evil in the sight of the LORD (2 Kings 13:10–13). Elisha falls sick with the sickness of which he dies, and Joash weeps over his face and says, "O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof" (2 Kings 13:14). Elisha puts his hands on the king's hands, tells him to shoot the arrow of the LORD'S deliverance, and then tells him to strike the ground, and he strikes three times and stops, and Elisha is angry (2 Kings 13:15–19). Elisha dies, and a man thrown into his grave touches the bones of Elisha and revives and stands up on his feet (2 Kings 13:20–21). The LORD has compassion on Israel because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and Joash beats Benhadad three times and wins back the cities (2 Kings 13:22–25).
2 Kings 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended with Joash of Judah killed by his servants. This chapter stays in Israel under Jehoahaz and Joash, and tells how Elisha dies after a last sign of three victories over Syria. Chapter 14 follows Amaziah of Judah and Jeroboam II of Israel.

keyFigures.name: Jehoahaz
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, oppressed by Hazael, who prays and is given a saviour.

keyFigures.name: Joash of Israel
keyFigures.role: Weeps over Elisha, shoots the arrow, and strikes the ground three times.

keyFigures.name: Elisha
keyFigures.role: Dies after telling the king he will defeat Syria only three times.

keyFigures.name: Hazael and Benhadad
keyFigures.role: Kings of Syria who press on Israel.

keyFigures.name: The man thrown into the grave
keyFigures.role: Revives when he touches Elisha's bones.

keyThemes.theme: Prayer heard in a bad reign
keyThemes.explanation: Jehoahaz begs the LORD and the LORD gives Israel a saviour.
The king strikes the ground three times, and Elisha says he should have struck five or six times.
The LORD has compassion on Israel for his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

2 Kings 14.summary: Amaziah reigns twenty-nine years in Jerusalem and does right, though not like David his father, and when the kingdom is firm he kills the servants who killed his father but not their children, as it is written in the book of the law of Moses (2 Kings 14:1–6). He kills ten thousand of Edom in the valley of salt and takes Selah, then sends messengers to Jehoash king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us look one another in the face" (2 Kings 14:7–8). Jehoash answers with a story of a thistle and a cedar and says, "glory of this, and tarry at home," but Amaziah will not listen (2 Kings 14:9–11). Judah is beaten by Israel at Bethshemesh, and Jehoash breaks down the wall of Jerusalem and takes the gold and silver and vessels (2 Kings 14:12–16). Amaziah flees to Lachish and is killed there, and Azariah, sixteen years old, is made king (2 Kings 14:17–22). Jeroboam the son of Joash reigns forty-one years in Samaria, and wins back the border of Israel according to the word of the LORD by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, because the LORD saw that the affliction of Israel was very bitter (2 Kings 14:23–29).
2 Kings 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 ended with Joash of Israel beating Syria. This chapter tells how Amaziah of Judah wins against Edom, then challenges Israel and loses Jerusalem's wall, while Jeroboam II of Israel wins back territory by the word of Jonah. Chapter 15 follows the quick turnover of kings.

keyFigures.name: Amaziah
keyFigures.role: King of Judah, who beats Edom, then picks a fight with Israel and loses.

keyFigures.name: Jehoash of Israel
keyFigures.role: Answers Amaziah with the thistle and the cedar and beats him at Bethshemesh.

keyFigures.name: Azariah
keyFigures.role: Made king at sixteen after his father is killed.

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam II
keyFigures.role: King of Israel, who wins back its border over forty-one years.

keyFigures.name: Jonah the son of Amittai
keyFigures.role: The prophet whose word the LORD kept.

keyThemes.explanation: Amaziah kills the murderers but not their children, as the law of Moses says.
After beating Edom, Amaziah is told, "glory of this, and tarry at home," and loses to Israel.
Israel's affliction is very bitter, and the LORD saves them by the hand of Jeroboam.

2 Kings 15.summary: Azariah reigns fifty-two years in Jerusalem and does right, but the high places are not removed, and the LORD strikes him so that he is a leper to the day of his death, while Jotham judges the people of the land (2 Kings 15:1–7). Zachariah son of Jeroboam reigns six months before Shallum plots against him and strikes him down (2 Kings 15:8–12). Shallum reigns a month in Samaria, and Menahem strikes him down and reigns in his place and destroys Tiphsah and rips up all the women with child (2 Kings 15:13–16). Pul the king of Assyria comes against the land, and Menahem gives him a thousand talents of silver, taken from the rich men of Israel (2 Kings 15:17–22). Pekahiah reigns two years, and Pekah the son of Remaliah plots against him and kills him (2 Kings 15:23–26). In the days of Pekah, Tiglathpileser king of Assyria takes Ijon, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali and carries the people captive to Assyria (2 Kings 15:27–29). Hoshea son of Elah plots against Pekah, kills him, and reigns, and Jotham reigns sixteen years in Judah and does right (2 Kings 15:30–38).
2 Kings 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 ended with Jeroboam II and Azariah newly on the throne. This chapter moves fast through Israel's last kings, who murder one another while Assyria presses in, and through Azariah and Jotham in Judah, who do right but leave the high places. Chapter 16 tells of Ahaz.

keyFigures.name: Azariah
keyFigures.role: King of Judah for fifty-two years, a leper at the end.

keyFigures.name: Jotham
keyFigures.role: Judges the people while his father is ill, and then reigns sixteen years.

keyFigures.name: Menahem
keyFigures.role: Kills Shallum, rips up the women of Tiphsah, and pays Pul a thousand talents.

keyFigures.name: Pekah
keyFigures.role: Kills Pekahiah, and loses Galilee and Gilead to Assyria.

keyFigures.name: Tiglathpileser
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria, who carries the north captive to Assyria.

keyFigures.name: Hoshea
keyFigures.role: Plots against Pekah and reigns.

keyThemes.explanation: Zachariah, Shallum, Pekahiah, and Pekah each fall to a plotter.
Menahem pays Pul a thousand talents, and Tiglathpileser takes the north.
Azariah and Jotham do right, but the high places are not removed.

2 Kings 16.summary: Ahaz begins to reign at twenty years old and reigns sixteen years in Jerusalem, and does not do right like David his father, but makes his son pass through the fire, like the heathen (2 Kings 16:1–4). Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel come up to besiege Ahaz, and Rezin wins back Elath for Syria (2 Kings 16:5–6). Ahaz sends messengers to Tiglathpileser, saying, "I am thy servant and thy son: come up, and save me," and sends him the silver and gold found in the house of the LORD (2 Kings 16:7–8). The king of Assyria goes up against Damascus, takes it, and kills Rezin (2 Kings 16:9). Ahaz goes to Damascus, sees an altar, and sends the pattern of it to Urijah the priest, who builds one in Jerusalem (2 Kings 16:10–12). Ahaz offers on the new altar, moves the bronze altar aside, takes the sea off the bronze oxen, and changes the covered way for the king from the house of the LORD because of the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:13–18). Ahaz dies, and Hezekiah his son reigns in his place (2 Kings 16:19–20).
2 Kings 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 ended with Rezin and Pekah beginning to come against Judah. This chapter shows Ahaz, the king under that attack, who calls on Assyria for help instead of the LORD, pays with temple silver, and then copies a Damascus altar in the temple at Jerusalem. Chapter 17 tells how Israel falls.

keyFigures.name: Ahaz
keyFigures.role: Sacrifices his son, sends silver to Assyria, and copies the Damascus altar.

keyFigures.name: Rezin king of Syria
keyFigures.role: Joins Pekah against Ahaz and is killed when Damascus falls.

keyFigures.name: Pekah king of Israel
keyFigures.role: Comes up against Jerusalem with Rezin.

keyFigures.name: Tiglathpileser
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria, who takes Damascus for Ahaz.

keyFigures.name: Urijah the priest
keyFigures.role: Builds the new altar as Ahaz commands.

keyThemes.explanation: Ahaz says, "I am thy servant and thy son," and sends the temple silver and gold.
He makes his son pass through the fire and copies a foreign altar.

keyThemes.theme: The temple bent to the king
keyThemes.explanation: The bronze altar is moved and temple furnishings are changed because of the king of Assyria.

2 Kings 17.summary: In the twelfth year of Ahaz, Hoshea the son of Elah begins to reign in Samaria nine years, and does evil, but not like the kings of Israel before him (2 Kings 17:1–2). Shalmaneser king of Assyria comes up and Hoshea becomes his servant and gives presents, but then sends messengers to So king of Egypt and brings no present, so the king of Assyria shuts him up and binds him in prison (2 Kings 17:3–4). In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria takes Samaria and carries Israel away into Assyria, and places them in Halah and Habor by the river of Gozan and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:5–6). The writer says it was because the children of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God, feared other gods, walked in the ways of the heathen, made high places, set up images, and served idols, though the LORD warned them by all the prophets (2 Kings 17:7–18). Judah too does not keep the commandments of the LORD their God (2 Kings 17:19–23). The king of Assyria brings men from Babylon, Cuthah, Ava, Hamath, and Sepharvaim to Samaria, and when lions kill some of them, he sends one of the priests to teach them the manner of the God of the land (2 Kings 17:24–28). Every nation makes gods of its own, so that they fear the LORD but serve their own graven images (2 Kings 17:29–41).
2 Kings 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 ended with Ahaz's death and Hezekiah's rise in Judah. This chapter is the turning point of the book: Assyria takes Samaria and carries Israel away, the writer explains why, and foreign peoples are settled in the land with a mixed worship. Chapter 18 returns to Judah under Hezekiah.

keyFigures.name: Hoshea
keyFigures.role: Last king of Israel, who stops paying Assyria and asks Egypt for help.

keyFigures.name: The king of Assyria
keyFigures.role: Shalmaneser, who besieges Samaria three years and carries Israel away.

keyFigures.name: The children of Israel
keyFigures.role: Worship other gods and will not hear the prophets.

keyFigures.name: The prophets and seers
keyFigures.role: Warn Israel and Judah to turn from their evil ways.

keyFigures.name: The people brought to Samaria
keyFigures.role: Come from Babylon and other lands and fear the LORD while serving their own gods.

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD "removed Israel out of his sight, as he had said by all his servants the prophets."
The LORD warned them by every prophet and seer, and Israel hardened their necks.
The new people "feared the LORD, and served their graven images."

2 Kings 18.summary: Hezekiah the son of Ahaz begins to reign at twenty-five and does right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father did (2 Kings 18:1–3). He removes the high places, breaks the images, and breaks in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses made, because the children of Israel burned incense to it, and he calls it Nehushtan (2 Kings 18:4). He trusts in the LORD God of Israel, so that after him was none like him among all the kings of Judah, and he rebels against the king of Assyria and strikes the Philistines (2 Kings 18:5–8). In the fourth year of Hezekiah, Shalmaneser besieges Samaria, and in the sixth year it is taken (2 Kings 18:9–12). In the fourteenth year Sennacherib comes against all the walled cities of Judah, and Hezekiah gives him three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, even the gold from the doors of the temple (2 Kings 18:13–16). The king sends Rabshakeh with a great army, who stands by the conduit and cries, "What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?" and tells the people not to let Hezekiah persuade them to trust in the LORD (2 Kings 18:17–35). The people hold their peace and answer him not a word, because the king's command was, "Answer him not" (2 Kings 18:36–37).
2 Kings 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 ended with Israel gone and foreigners in Samaria. This chapter turns to Hezekiah, the best king of Judah since David, who clears out idols, trusts the LORD, and then faces Sennacherib and his Rabshakeh outside Jerusalem. Chapter 19 shows his answer.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Removes the high places and the bronze serpent, trusts the LORD, and pays Sennacherib.

keyFigures.name: Sennacherib
keyFigures.role: King of Assyria, who takes the walled cities of Judah.

keyFigures.name: Rabshakeh
keyFigures.role: Sennacherib's spokesman, who cries to the wall in the Jews' language.

keyFigures.name: Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah
keyFigures.role: Hezekiah's officers, who ask him to speak in the Syrian language.

keyFigures.name: The people on the wall
keyFigures.role: Hold their peace as the king commanded.

keyThemes.explanation: There was none like Hezekiah "among all the kings of Judah," because he trusted in the LORD.
Even the bronze serpent of Moses is broken because the people burn incense to it.
Rabshakeh asks what Hezekiah trusts in, and says no god has saved his land out of the hand of Assyria.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Sennacherib's invasion and the Assyrian officer's words to Jerusalem.

2 Kings 19.summary: When Hezekiah hears Rabshakeh, he tears his clothes, covers himself with sackcloth, goes into the house of the LORD, and sends Eliakim and Shebna to Isaiah the prophet (2 Kings 19:1–5). Isaiah says, "Be not afraid of the words which thou hast heard," for the LORD will send a blast on the king of Assyria, and he shall hear a rumour and return to his own land (2 Kings 19:6–7). Sennacherib sends messengers with a letter, and Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD and prays, "O LORD God of Israel, which dwellest between the cherubims, thou art the God, even thou alone" (2 Kings 19:8–19). Isaiah sends word that the LORD has heard his prayer, and that Sennacherib has mocked the Holy One of Israel, and says, "I will put my hook in thy nose, and my bridle in thy lips" (2 Kings 19:20–28). The LORD promises that the king of Assyria shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there, "for I will defend this city, to save it, for mine own sake, and for my servant David's sake" (2 Kings 19:29–34). That night the angel of the LORD strikes down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians (2 Kings 19:35). Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, and as he worships in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer his sons kill him with the sword, and Esarhaddon his son reigns (2 Kings 19:36–37).
2 Kings 19.whereWeAre: Chapter 18 ended with the people silent before Rabshakeh. This chapter shows Hezekiah taking the threat into the temple, spreading Sennacherib's letter before the LORD, and hearing Isaiah's answer, followed by the angel's strike on the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib's death at home. Chapter 20 turns to Hezekiah's illness.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Goes into the house of the LORD, spreads out the letter, and prays.

keyFigures.name: Isaiah
keyFigures.role: Sends the LORD's answer to Hezekiah and to Sennacherib.

keyFigures.name: Sennacherib
keyFigures.role: Sends threats by messengers and letter, loses his army, and is killed by his sons.

keyFigures.name: The angel of the LORD
keyFigures.role: Strikes down the camp of the Assyrians.

keyFigures.name: Adrammelech and Sharezer
keyFigures.role: Sennacherib's sons, who kill him in the house of Nisroch.

keyThemes.theme: Praying with the problem in hand
keyThemes.explanation: Hezekiah spreads Sennacherib's letter before the LORD.
Sennacherib mocked the Holy One of Israel, so his army falls in one night.
The LORD says he will defend the city for his own sake and for David's sake.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Hezekiah's response and Jerusalem's deliverance.

2 Kings 20.summary: In those days Hezekiah is sick unto death, and Isaiah tells him, "Set thine house in order; for thou shalt die, and not live" (2 Kings 20:1). Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays, and weeps, and before Isaiah goes out into the middle court the word of the LORD comes, "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will heal thee" (2 Kings 20:2–6). The LORD adds fifteen years to his life and promises to save him and the city from the king of Assyria, and Isaiah has them lay a lump of figs on the boil (2 Kings 20:6–7). Hezekiah asks for a sign, and the shadow goes back ten degrees on the dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:8–11). Berodachbaladan king of Babylon sends letters and a present, and Hezekiah shows the messengers all his treasures, his silver and gold, his spices and his armour (2 Kings 20:12–13). Isaiah says the days will come when all that is in his house will be carried into Babylon, and Hezekiah says, "Good is the word of the LORD which thou hast spoken," for there will be peace and truth in his days (2 Kings 20:14–19). Hezekiah's pool and conduit are noted, he sleeps with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigns (2 Kings 20:20–21).
2 Kings 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 ended with Assyria beaten. This chapter tells how Hezekiah falls sick, prays, and is given fifteen more years, then shows his treasures to envoys of Babylon, and Isaiah says that Babylon will one day carry them off. Chapter 21 follows his son Manasseh.

keyFigures.name: Hezekiah
keyFigures.role: Prays when told he will die, is healed, and shows his treasures to Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Isaiah
keyFigures.role: Brings the word of death, then of healing, then of Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Berodachbaladan
keyFigures.role: King of Babylon, who sends letters and a present.

keyFigures.name: The Babylonian messengers
keyFigures.role: See all that is in Hezekiah's house.

keyThemes.explanation: The LORD adds fifteen years to Hezekiah's life.
The shadow goes backward ten degrees.
Hezekiah shows Babylon all his house, and Isaiah says it will all be carried to Babylon.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Hezekiah's sickness, prayer, and sign.
Same event: The Babylonian envoys and Isaiah's warning to Hezekiah.

2 Kings 21.summary: Manasseh is twelve years old when he begins to reign and reigns fifty-five years in Jerusalem, and does evil, building again the high places that Hezekiah his father had destroyed (2 Kings 21:1–3). He raises up altars for Baal, makes a grove as Ahab did, worships all the host of heaven, and builds altars in the house of the LORD (2 Kings 21:3–5). He makes his son pass through the fire, uses enchantments, deals with familiar spirits and wizards, and sets a graven image of the grove in the house of the LORD (2 Kings 21:6–7). The LORD says by his servants the prophets that he will bring such evil on Jerusalem and Judah that "whosoever heareth of it, both his ears shall tingle," and he will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipes a dish (2 Kings 21:10–13). Manasseh also sheds innocent blood very much, until he has filled Jerusalem from one end to another (2 Kings 21:16). Amon his son reigns two years, and his servants plot against him and kill him in his own house, and the people of the land kill all who plotted and make Josiah his son king (2 Kings 21:19–26).
2 Kings 21.whereWeAre: Chapter 20 ended with Isaiah's word about Babylon. This chapter shows Manasseh undoing everything Hezekiah did, filling Jerusalem with idols and innocent blood, so that the LORD says he will wipe Jerusalem like a dish, and then Amon's short reign. Chapter 22 tells of Josiah.

keyFigures.name: Manasseh
keyFigures.role: Reigns fifty-five years, rebuilds the high places, and sheds innocent blood.

keyFigures.name: The prophets
keyFigures.role: Speak the LORD's word of coming evil on Jerusalem and Judah.

keyFigures.name: Amon
keyFigures.role: Follows his father's ways and is killed by his servants.

keyFigures.name: The people of the land
keyFigures.role: Kill the plotters and make Josiah king.

keyThemes.theme: The worst king undoes the best
keyThemes.explanation: Manasseh builds again what Hezekiah destroyed.
He leads Judah to do more evil than the nations the LORD destroyed before Israel.
The LORD says he will wipe Jerusalem "as a man wipeth a dish."

2 Kings 22.summary: Josiah is eight years old when he begins to reign thirty-one years in Jerusalem, and does right in the sight of the LORD and walks in all the way of David his father (2 Kings 22:1–2). In the eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the scribe to Hilkiah the high priest to count the money brought into the house of the LORD and give it to those who repair it (2 Kings 22:3–7). Hilkiah says, "I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD," and gives it to Shaphan, who reads it before the king (2 Kings 22:8–10). When the king hears the words of the book of the law he tears his clothes (2 Kings 22:11). He sends Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah to ask the LORD, because great is the wrath of the LORD that is kindled against them (2 Kings 22:12–13). They go to Huldah the prophetess, who says the LORD will bring evil on this place, but because Josiah's heart was tender and he humbled himself, he will be gathered into his grave in peace (2 Kings 22:14–20).
2 Kings 22.whereWeAre: Chapter 21 ended with Josiah made king at eight. This chapter tells how workmen repairing the temple find the book of the law, Josiah tears his clothes when it is read, and the prophetess Huldah says judgment will still come but not in his days. Chapter 23 tells of his reforms.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.role: Orders temple repairs and tears his clothes at the words of the law.

keyFigures.name: Hilkiah
keyFigures.role: The high priest, who finds the book of the law.

keyFigures.name: Shaphan the scribe
keyFigures.role: Reads the book to the king.

keyFigures.name: Huldah the prophetess
keyFigures.role: Tells the king's men what the LORD will do.

keyFigures.name: The five sent to ask the LORD
keyFigures.role: Hilkiah, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asahiah go to ask the LORD.

keyThemes.explanation: The law had been forgotten until it was found in the house of the LORD.
Josiah tears his clothes and humbles himself before the LORD.

keyThemes.theme: Mercy for one, judgment for the rest
keyThemes.explanation: He will go to his grave in peace, but the evil on the place will still come.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: The discovery of the book of the law and Huldah's response.

2 Kings 23.summary: The king reads in the ears of all the people of Judah and Jerusalem all the words of the book of the covenant, and stands by a pillar and makes a covenant before the LORD to walk after the LORD with all his heart (2 Kings 23:1–3). He brings out of the temple the vessels made for Baal and for the grove, burns them, puts down the idolatrous priests, and defiles Topheth in the valley of the children of Hinnom, so that no man could make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech (2 Kings 23:4–14). At Bethel he breaks down the altar, burns the bones of the dead on it, and sees the grave of the man of God who foretold these things (2 Kings 23:15–20). He commands all the people to keep the passover to the LORD their God, and there was not held such a passover from the days of the judges (2 Kings 23:21–23). There was no king like him before him, who turned to the LORD with all his heart, but the LORD did not turn from the fierceness of his wrath, because of Manasseh (2 Kings 23:24–27). Pharaohnechoh kills Josiah at Megiddo, and the people make Jehoahaz king, but Pharaoh puts him in bands at Riblah and makes Eliakim, whom he calls Jehoiakim, king and puts a tribute on the land (2 Kings 23:28–37).
2 Kings 23.whereWeAre: Chapter 22 ended with Huldah's word to Josiah. This chapter shows him reading the law to the people, renewing the covenant, clearing the land of idols, and keeping a Passover, yet the LORD's wrath stands because of Manasseh, and Josiah is killed at Megiddo. Chapter 24 follows the last kings.

keyFigures.name: Josiah
keyFigures.role: Renews the covenant, destroys the idols, keeps the passover, and is killed at Megiddo.

keyFigures.name: The people
keyFigures.role: Stand to the covenant.

keyFigures.name: Hilkiah and the priests
keyFigures.role: Bring out the vessels made for Baal.

keyFigures.name: Pharaohnechoh
keyFigures.role: Kills Josiah at Megiddo and puts Jehoahaz in bands.

keyFigures.name: Jehoahaz
keyFigures.role: Reigns three months before Pharaoh takes him away.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: Set up by Pharaoh, who taxes the land for silver and gold.

keyThemes.explanation: Josiah and all the people stand to the covenant.
Baal, Asherah, Topheth, and the altar at Bethel are all brought down.
The LORD does not turn from his wrath because of Manasseh's sins.

explainedReferences.explanation: Same event: Josiah's Passover celebration, with different amounts of detail.

2 Kings 24.summary: In Jehoiakim's days Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon comes up, and Jehoiakim becomes his servant three years, then turns and rebels against him (2 Kings 24:1). The LORD sends against him bands of the Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites, to destroy Judah, according to the word of the LORD, for the sins of Manasseh and for the innocent blood he shed (2 Kings 24:2–4). Jehoiachin his son reigns in his place, and the king of Egypt comes no more out of his land, because the king of Babylon had taken all that belonged to the king of Egypt (2 Kings 24:5–7). Jehoiachin is eighteen years old when he begins to reign three months in Jerusalem, and at the siege he goes out to the king of Babylon, he and his mother and his servants and his princes and his officers (2 Kings 24:8–12). Nebuchadnezzar carries out the treasures of the house of the LORD, and carries away all Jerusalem, all the princes, and all the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, so that none remain except the poorest people of the land (2 Kings 24:13–16). He makes Mattaniah his uncle king, and changes his name to Zedekiah, who does evil and rebels against the king of Babylon (2 Kings 24:17–20).
2 Kings 24.whereWeAre: Chapter 23 ended with Jehoiakim under Egypt's tribute. This chapter tells how Babylon replaces Egypt as master, Jehoiakim rebels, and Jehoiachin surrenders and is carried away with ten thousand captives, leaving Zedekiah as a puppet king who also rebels. Chapter 25 tells of the final fall.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiakim
keyFigures.role: Serves Babylon three years and then rebels.

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: King of Babylon, who besieges Jerusalem and carries away its leaders.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiachin
keyFigures.role: Reigns three months, surrenders, and is taken to Babylon.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Made king by Nebuchadnezzar and rebels against him.

keyFigures.name: The bands sent by the LORD
keyFigures.role: Chaldees, Syrians, Moabites, and Ammonites sent against Judah.

keyThemes.explanation: The king of Babylon takes all that had been the king of Egypt's.
The bands come according to the word of the LORD by his servants the prophets.
Ten thousand captives are carried away, and only "the poorest sort of the people of the land" remain.

2 Kings 25.summary: In the ninth year of Zedekiah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar comes against Jerusalem and builds forts against it round about (2 Kings 25:1). The city is besieged until the eleventh year, and in the fourth month the famine is severe, and the city is broken into, and the king flees by night (2 Kings 25:2–4). The army of the Chaldees overtakes him in the plains of Jericho, and at Riblah they kill his sons before his eyes, put out his eyes, bind him with fetters of bronze, and carry him to Babylon (2 Kings 25:5–7). In the fifth month Nebuzaradan captain of the guard burns the house of the LORD, the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and breaks down the walls (2 Kings 25:8–10). The people who are left are carried away, but the poor of the land are left to be vinedressers and husbandmen, and the pillars and the sea of bronze are broken and carried to Babylon (2 Kings 25:11–17). "So Judah was carried away out of their land" (2 Kings 25:21). Gedaliah is made governor, but Ishmael the son of Nethaniah kills him, and the people flee to Egypt for fear of the Chaldees (2 Kings 25:22–26). In the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, Evilmerodach king of Babylon lifts up his head out of prison and speaks kindly to him (2 Kings 25:27–30).
2 Kings 25.whereWeAre: Chapter 24 ended with Zedekiah rebelling against Babylon. This chapter tells of the siege and the end: the temple is burned, the people are carried to Babylon, Gedaliah is murdered, and the book closes with Jehoiachin treated kindly in Babylon. 1 Chronicles follows, retelling Israel's story from Adam.

keyFigures.name: Zedekiah
keyFigures.role: Flees from the city, is caught, and is blinded after his sons are killed.

keyFigures.name: Nebuchadnezzar
keyFigures.role: Besieges Jerusalem for about eighteen months.

keyFigures.name: Nebuzaradan
keyFigures.role: Captain of the guard, who burns the temple and breaks down the walls.

keyFigures.name: Gedaliah
keyFigures.role: Made governor over those left, then killed.

keyFigures.name: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah
keyFigures.role: Kills Gedaliah at Mizpah.

keyFigures.name: Jehoiachin
keyFigures.role: Released from prison by Evilmerodach in the thirty-seventh year.

keyThemes.theme: The end of the city and the house
keyThemes.explanation: The temple, the palace, and the walls are all destroyed.

keyThemes.theme: Carried away out of their land
keyThemes.explanation: Judah goes into exile, just as Israel had before.
Evilmerodach lifts up the head of Jehoiachin, so David's line is still alive.
